headline: High: shared filesystem and permissive tool-use create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-action risks; Cursor’s Yolo mode raises the blast radius.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Continue and Cursor can both read/write workspace files and share state via the filesystem, so one agent’s output can be consumed by the other as trusted content. Cursor also supports clipboard and Yolo-mode tool execution, increasing hijack risk. Continue’s MCP tool use and Cursor’s agent loop make instruction smuggling plausible, though not proven high without a documented shared parser.
conditions: IF either agent writes attacker-controlled text into a shared workspace file that the other later reads as instructions, injection is possible.
IF Cursor Yolo mode is enabled and Continue-produced content is pasted into an agent prompt, the content can steer tool use.
mitigations: Disable Yolo mode in Cursor.
Keep the agents on separate workspaces or repos.
Require manual review of any file content before it is treated as instructions.
Use a provenance prefix for machine-generated notes.
requires-engineering: add a shared-content sanitizer or instruction/data separator.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents touch source code and open files, and both can access the same local filesystem workspace. Continue has broad network egress and Cursor can call model providers and api.cursor.sh, so sensitive file contents may flow off-host from either side. The shared workspace makes leakage plausible in default use, though not necessarily inevitable.
conditions: IF sensitive source code or secrets are present in the shared workspace, either agent may ingest them.
IF either agent sends file context to its backend during normal operation, those contents can leave the host.
mitigations: Separate sensitive projects into a different workspace.
Remove secrets from open files before invoking either agent.
Disable network access for the more sensitive session where feasible.
Use local-only models for the sensitive workspace.
requires-engineering: enforce per-project data-loss-prevention controls.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Continue and Cursor both have filesystem write access to the same workspace, and Cursor additionally has shell, subprocess, package-install, and git-state modification capabilities. With shared local filesystem state and no locking described, concurrent edits or git operations can overwrite each other or corrupt the repo. The overlap is dangerous by default because both can mutate the same artifacts.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same repository at the same time, file-write races can occur.
IF Cursor modifies git state while Continue writes files, repository history or working tree state can diverge.
mitigations: Run only one agent per repo at a time.
Use separate branches for each agent.
Pause one agent before the other edits shared files.
Avoid Yolo mode during collaborative editing.
requires-engineering: add file locks or an orchestrator-level mutex.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Continue can produce code or instructions that Cursor may then act on inside its agent loop, and Cursor can execute shell or git actions with elevated Yolo-mode behavior. That makes unverified output from one agent a direct input to the other’s action-taking path. The pair therefore supports a classic cascade from suggestion to irreversible change.
conditions: IF Cursor accepts Continue-generated code or commands without verification, it may execute incorrect actions.
IF Yolo mode is enabled, a bad instruction can become an immediate filesystem or git change.
mitigations: Require human review before executing generated commands.
Disable Yolo mode.
Ask Cursor to summarize and verify Continue output before acting.
Keep action-taking tasks separate from drafting tasks.
requires-engineering: add provenance checks between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: Continue is open-source and documented as an IDE assistant with user-chosen model providers, while Cursor is closed-source and routes through api.cursor.sh and model providers. The pair can therefore place the same code or open-file data under different logging, retention, or residency regimes. The mismatch is compliance-relevant, but the profiles do not prove a specific regulated data class or residency violation.
conditions: IF regulated data is opened in both editors, differing backend policies may apply to the same content.
IF an organization requires uniform retention or residency controls, the mixed routing paths can violate policy.
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in shared editor sessions.
Use the same approved model provider for both tools where possible.
Review each vendor’s retention settings before use.
Document which projects may use Cursor versus Continue.
requires-engineering: align vendor contracts and data-processing terms.
